name: Uma Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head stockwoman at Hollins Farm, which the Aldridge family has farmed for four generations. We've got 300 breeding ewes, 40 Hereford cows and about 150 hectares of wheat and barley. I'm up at half five, check the stock, feed the cows in the shed in winter, and then it's whatever the day needs: lambing, tagging, moving sheep, helping old Mr Aldridge with the hay.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work, and that the Aldridges treat me like family. What wears me out is that money is always short; the farm can't pay much and I don't expect it to. My fiancé Josef is a herdsman on Kerr's dairy next door, we're getting married next August at St Michael's, and the wedding has eaten what little we'd saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype? That sounds about right to me. Most things that come out of the city are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my grandad used to say: you can't plough with a newspaper. At church I'd say farming will be here long after the gadgets. I don't go online much, so that's where it'd stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, my worries are the same as now. Money for the wedding, money for a house one day, and whether Hollins can keep going when Mr Aldridge's son takes over. AI fizzling out doesn't change any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as I do. Josef and I would cut the wedding down a bit, maybe a buffet in the church hall instead of the hotel. And we'd put aside whatever we can, even fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. A bit tight in the chest when I think about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Mr Aldridge's son taking over. What worries you about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robert's a good man, but he went to university in the city and likes figures more than animals. He might want to cut costs, and the head stockwoman is a cost. I pray he keeps Hollins the way it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would cutting the wedding back mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd sting a bit, I'll admit. But a wedding is a promise in front of God, not a party. Josef and I can have a good marriage on sandwiches in the church hall.

say: I'd say what my grandad said: **you can't plough** with a newspaper.
At church I'd say **farming** will outlast the gadgets.
think: My worries stay the same: **wedding money** and a future house.
I wonder if Hollins keeps going when **Robert Aldridge** takes over.
do: Keep working as she does at **Hollins Farm**.
Cut the wedding to a **church hall buffet**.
Put aside **fifty a month** with Josef.
feel: **Settled**, with a tight chest about money.
S0.quote: Josef and I can have a good marriage on sandwiches in the church hall.
fieldNote: Her **faith** frames how she sees both money and change.
The owner's son **Robert** is a quiet worry.
The **wedding** is her main financial pressure.

steps.text: Keep running the ewes and Herefords at Hollins Farm
Move the wedding reception to a church hall buffet
Save fifty a month with Josef

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds closer to what people keep talking about. I'd believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine for offices, but sheep still need a shepherd. At the mart I'd say the same. I'd say we shouldn't let computers decide everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's Josef I'd think of. Kerr's dairy has already been looking at robot milkers, and if those spread, my fiancé's job is the first to go. My own job is hands-on, so I'm all right for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Josef and I would save harder and move the wedding to the church hall for sure. I'd ask my mum and dad if we could live with them for a year after the wedding, to save for a deposit. I'd keep my head down and work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, for Josef. It sits in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Josef do if Kerr's dairy brought in robot milkers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Josef says he'd look after the robots. But Kerr's would only need one person for that, and Mr Kerr's nephew is already lined up. I don't like to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try using AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I don't trust it and I don't need it. Mr Aldridge has managed without it for fifty years and so have I.

say: I'd say it's fine for **offices**, but sheep still need a **shepherd**.
I'd say we shouldn't let **computers decide** everything.
think: **Josef's job** is first to go if robot milkers spread.
My own work is **hands-on**, so I'm all right for a while.
do: **Save harder** and hold the wedding in the church hall.
Ask her parents to let them **live with them** for a year.
feel: **Worried** for Josef, sitting in her stomach.
S1.quote: Kerr's dairy has already been looking at robot milkers, and if those spread, my fiancé's job is the first to go.
fieldNote: Her worry is for her **fiancé**, a household earner, more than herself.
She **refuses AI** outright and is proud of it.
**Family support** is her chosen safety net.

steps.text: Save harder with Josef for a house deposit
Hold the wedding reception in the St Michael's church hall
Ask her parents if she and Josef can live with them for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. Robots by 2031. I don't like the sound of that at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is people playing God, and I'd say it at church. I'd say families and communities need to look after each other, because nobody else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Josef loses his job by 2031 and I could lose mine soon after. If Robert takes over Hollins and robots are cheaper, he'll buy them. Josef and I would be newly married with nothing saved and both out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd marry sooner, at St Michael's, quiet, so we can live together and save on rent. We'd move in with my parents. I'd keep working at Hollins every day until they tell me otherwise, and I'd cut everything, no car, no extras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if I'm honest. I pray a lot more, picturing that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between the AI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years to get married and get settled before the robots come for the stock work. It's a bit of breathing room. But I don't see what we'd do with it except save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, and the church. My dad's a builder, and he says there's always work for someone who'll get their hands dirty. I hope he's right, but I don't know if he is any more.

say: I'd call it **people playing God** and say so at church.
I'd say **families and communities** must look after each other.
think: **Josef** loses his job by 2031 and I could follow.
If Robert takes over, he'll **buy robots** if they're cheaper.
do: **Marry sooner**, quietly, to share a home and save rent.
**Cut everything**, including the car, and work until told to stop.
S2.quote: Josef and I would be newly married with nothing saved and both out of work.
fieldNote: Both household jobs are **hands-on** and exposed after 2031.
Her responses are **faith and family**, not retraining.
She sees the **three-year gap** only as time to save.

steps.text: Bring the wedding forward to a quiet service at St Michael's
Move in with her parents after the wedding
Give up the car and all extras

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Robots by 2034. That's still soon for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to keep farms in family hands, not companies with robots. I'd say it at church and to anyone at the mart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years gives us a little more time, but I think the end is the same. Josef would go first, then me. We'd be thirty-two with maybe a child and no work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd marry as planned and live with my parents for a couple of years. Josef would look for work with my dad's building firm, which feels steadier. I'd stay at Hollins and save every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Frightened still, but I'd have time to pray on it and plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned maybe a child. Would this change those plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still want children, because that's what a family is for. But maybe we'd wait until we know what's coming. That hurts to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Robert Aldridge, if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Robert that Hollins has always been about people, his family and mine. Robots won't come to old Mr Aldridge's funeral. I hope Robert remembers that.

say: I'd say farms should stay in **family hands**, not companies.
I'd say it at **church** and at the mart.
think: Five years gives **more time**, but the end is the same.
We'd be thirty-two, maybe with **a child**, and no work.
do: **Marry as planned** and live with her parents for a couple of years.
Have Josef look for work at her **dad's building firm**.
Stay at Hollins and **save every month**.
feel: **Heavy** and frightened, but with time to pray and plan.
S3.quote: Robots won't come to old Mr Aldridge's funeral.
fieldNote: She'd **delay children**, which she finds painful to admit.
**Loyalty** to the Aldridge family runs deep.
Her plan shifts **Josef** into her dad's building trade as the steadier option.

steps.text: Wait to have children until the robot timeline is clearer
Get Josef work with her dad's building firm
Save every month from her Hollins wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's better. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for families and communities to get ready, and I'd say it at church. I'd say we shouldn't wait for the government to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like enough to build a home and start a family. Hollins might change, but I'd have time. I still don't think I'd learn to work with robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd marry, live with my parents for a year, and save for a deposit. I'd keep working at Hollins. I'd vote for whoever promises to keep family farms and apprenticeships going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's further off. I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Hollins brought in robots in 2039, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to find another family farm that still wants a stockwoman. Or I'd stay home with the children, if we had them. I'd find a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you change your mind about learning to use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If old Mr Aldridge asked me to learn the AI, I'd do it for him, not for a company. But I'd still do the stock by eye.

say: I'd say families and communities have **time to get ready**.
I'd say we **shouldn't wait** for the government.
think: Ten years is enough to **build a home** and start a family.
I still **wouldn't learn** to work with robots.
do: **Marry**, live with her parents a year, and save for a deposit.
Vote for candidates who back **family farms** and apprenticeships.
feel: Worried, but able to **breathe** because it's further off.
S4.quote: If old Mr Aldridge asked me to learn the AI, I'd do it for him, not for a company.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her plan a **family**.
Her only route to AI is **loyalty** to the Aldridges.

steps.text: Save for a house deposit while living with her parents

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Josef and I would both lose our work just as we're starting out. What would help is keeping farms in family hands, and apprenticeships for young people to learn trades. Not handouts, just a chance to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of us out here lean on God more than on government. If the work goes, the church will still be there, and that's worth something.

headlineQuote: A lot of us out here lean on God more than on government.
portrait: Uma, 27, is **head stockwoman** on a four-generation family farm with sheep, cattle and grain.
She's engaged to Josef, a **dairy herdsman**, and their wedding has used up their savings.
She **never uses AI**, trusts family and church, and is loyal to the Aldridges.
Her biggest fear is that **both jobs** in her household are hands-on and exposed to robots.
Her mood rises to **alarmed** under fast AGI, and she would delay children.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Josef would both lose work as they start out.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** so young people can learn trades, not handouts.
